title: Career Roadmap: Service Designer
summary: A Service Designer designs and improves the complete experience people have when interacting with a service. They consider not only what a customer sees, but also the processes, employees, technology, communication and systems working behind the scenes.

facts.Current degree: Liberal Arts / Liberal Studies (BA / B.Sc Liberal Arts & Sciences)

about.label: Pathway
about.text: Liberal Arts / Liberal Studies – Design & Innovation Studies

blocks.text: A Service Designer designs and improves the complete experience people have when interacting with a service. They consider not only what a customer sees, but also the processes, employees, technology, communication and systems working behind the scenes.

For example, improving a hospital appointment system involves understanding how patients book appointments, how staff manage schedules, how doctors receive information and how patients get follow-up care.
Service Designers combine research, creativity, systems thinking and collaboration to make services more useful, accessible and efficient.
Typical responsibilities

items.text: Research customer needs, behaviours and pain points.
Map customer journeys and identify service gaps.
Design service experiences across digital and physical channels.
Create service blueprints showing front-stage and back-stage processes.
Facilitate workshops with customers, employees and stakeholders.
Prototype and test new service concepts.
Collaborate with UX designers, product managers, engineers and operations teams.
Measure whether service improvements deliver meaningful results.

blocks.text: Recommended undergraduate route

The specified pathway—Liberal Arts / Liberal Studies with a specialisation in Design & Innovation Studies—is suitable because service design draws on multiple disciplines, including design, psychology, sociology, business and technology.

rows.text: Class 11–12
Develop communication, observation, creative problem-solving and research skills. Any stream may be suitable, subject to college eligibility requirements.
Undergraduate years 1–2
Study design thinking, human-centred design, psychology, sociology, research methods and innovation.
Undergraduate years 2–3
Learn UX research, journey mapping, prototyping, systems thinking and service operations.
Undergraduate year 3 or 4, if applicable
Complete a service-design project, industry internship, research project or capstone.
After graduation
Apply for entry-level service design, UX research, customer experience or design research roles. Consider postgraduate study if it supports a specific career goal.

blocks.text: Related postgraduate options
A postgraduate qualification is optional, not universally required. Relevant options include:

items.text: Master’s in Service Design
Master’s in Interaction Design or UX Design
Master’s in Design Management
Master’s in Human-Computer Interaction
Master’s in Strategic Design or Innovation
Master’s in Human-Centred Design

blocks.text: Evaluate programmes based on studio work, research opportunities, industry projects, faculty expertise and graduate portfolios—not just the course title.
Year 1
Explore
Build foundational design and research skills

items.text: Learn design thinking and human-centred design.
Study basic psychology, sociology and consumer behaviour.
Practise observation, interviewing and note-taking.
Analyse everyday services such as public transport, banking or college administration.
Create a simple case study identifying a service problem and proposing improvements.

blocks.text: Year 2
Practise
Learn the service-design process

items.text: Conduct user interviews and contextual research.
Create personas, empathy maps and customer journey maps.
Learn service blueprints and stakeholder mapping.
Practise low-fidelity prototyping and usability testing.
Use Figma or similar tools to communicate service concepts.
Complete one end-to-end service redesign project.

blocks.text: Year 3
Apply
Work on realistic service challenges

items.text: Study systems thinking, accessibility and service operations.
Learn workshop facilitation and stakeholder communication.
Conduct field research with a real organisation or user group.
Apply for internships in UX research, design research, customer experience or innovation.
Develop a portfolio with two or three well-documented projects.

blocks.text: Year 4, if applicable
Specialise
Become employment-ready

items.text: Complete a capstone project involving research, service mapping, prototyping and evaluation.
Work with a company, NGO, public-service organisation or startup.
Learn to connect design recommendations to operational outcomes.
Refine portfolio case studies and practise presenting design decisions.
Apply for graduate roles and prepare for case-study interviews.

rows.text: User research
Interviews, observation, surveys and contextual inquiry
Service design
Customer journey mapping, service blueprints and touchpoint analysis
Design thinking
Problem framing, ideation, prototyping and testing
Systems thinking
Understanding how people, policies, processes and technology interact
Visual communication
Diagrams, journey maps, process maps and presentation design
UX fundamentals
Information architecture, usability and interaction design
Facilitation
Workshops, brainstorming, stakeholder interviews and collaboration
Analytical thinking
Synthesising research, prioritising pain points and evaluating outcomes
Communication
Presenting findings, writing design rationales and storytelling
Accessibility
Designing services that work for people with diverse needs and abilities

blocks.text: Figma
For service touchpoint concepts, wireframes, clickable prototypes and collaborative design workshops.
Miro or FigJam
For customer journey maps, stakeholder maps, affinity diagrams and service blueprints.
Google Forms or similar survey tools
For collecting structured feedback and exploring user needs.
Notion or similar documentation tools
For organising research findings, project documentation, insights and portfolio development.
Tool proficiency is useful, but employers will generally want to see how you investigate problems, develop solutions and validate your design decisions—not just which tools you use.
A Service Designer can work across several industries.

rows.text: Digital service design
Improving how people complete tasks across websites, apps and support channels
Healthcare service design
Improving patient journeys, appointment systems and hospital experiences
Financial services
Simplifying banking, insurance claims and customer onboarding
Public-service design
Making government services easier to access and understand
Education service design
Improving student admissions, enrolment and learning-support services
Retail and hospitality
Improving shopping, delivery, booking and after-sales experiences
Employee experience
Improving internal workplace services and employee processes
Sustainability and social innovation
Designing accessible, inclusive and environmentally responsible services

blocks.text: Common job titles to explore

items.text: Junior Service Designer
Service Design Intern
UX Research Assistant
Design Researcher
Customer Experience Designer
Experience Design Associate
Innovation Design Associate
Human-Centred Design Researcher

blocks.text: Some of these roles overlap with service design but have different responsibilities. Read each job description carefully.

sections.heading: Projects to Build a Strong Portfolio

blocks.text: Aim to complete at least three substantial projects. Clearly label student projects and avoid presenting hypothetical outcomes as real business results.

blocks.label: Project 1
blocks.text: Redesign a College Admissions Service
Research where applicants face difficulties, map the application journey, identify delays and propose improvements across online and offline interactions.

blocks.label: Deliverables
blocks.text: interview findings, journey map, service blueprint and proposed service flow.

blocks.label: Project 2
blocks.text: Improve a Patient Appointment Service
Investigate booking, waiting, communication and follow-up. Identify opportunities to reduce confusion and improve accessibility.

blocks.label: Deliverables
blocks.text: current-state journey, pain-point analysis, future-state blueprint and tested prototype.

blocks.label: Project 3
blocks.text: Improve a Public Transport Experience
Study how passengers discover routes, purchase tickets, navigate stations and handle disruptions.

blocks.label: Deliverables
blocks.text: field observations, stakeholder map, service improvements and an evaluation plan.
For every case study, explain the original problem, research method, key evidence, design decisions, prototype, testing results and limitations.
Search for opportunities under these titles:

items.text: Service Design Intern
UX Research Intern
Design Research Intern
Customer Experience Intern
Product Design Intern
Innovation or Design Strategy Intern

blocks.text: Potential places to explore include design consultancies, digital product companies, banks, healthcare organisations, government innovation initiatives, social-impact organisations and startups.
How to find opportunities in India:

items.text: Search company career pages and internship platforms using the titles above.
Approach local organisations with a focused service-improvement proposal.
Participate in design challenges, research projects and interdisciplinary hackathons.
Ask design faculty or community organisations for access to a real-world problem.
Document your contribution, methods and evidence rather than only the final screens.

blocks.text: Prioritise practical learning over collecting certificates.
Useful learning areas include:

items.text: Design thinking and human-centred design
UX research and usability testing
Service design methods and service blueprinting
Systems thinking and innovation
Accessibility and inclusive design
Qualitative research and interview techniques
Workshop facilitation and design storytelling

blocks.text: Look for courses from recognised universities, professional design organisations and established learning platforms. Verify the syllabus, practical assignments, instructor expertise and certificate terms before paying.
A possible career progression is:
Entry level
Service Design Intern / Junior Service Designer / Design Research Assistant
Early career
Service Designer / UX Researcher / Customer Experience Designer
Experienced professional
Senior Service Designer / Design Strategist / Service Design Lead
Leadership
Head of Service Design / Design Director / Experience Strategy Leader

Progression depends on the organisation, demonstrated impact, research capability, leadership skills and experience. Some professionals specialise in research or strategy instead of following a management track.
Service design is relevant wherever organisations need to improve connected experiences across people, processes and technology. Potential growth areas include:

items.text: AI-enabled customer services and human support workflows
Digital public services and citizen experience
Healthcare access and patient journeys
Inclusive and accessible service delivery
Omnichannel banking, retail and travel experiences
Employee experience and internal operations
Sustainable services and social innovation

blocks.text: A useful differentiator is the ability to evaluate whether a redesigned service actually improves outcomes—for example, reducing confusion, making a process more accessible or lowering avoidable support requests.
Preparation progress
0 of 9
Understand human-centred design and design thinking
Practise interviews, observation and qualitative research
Create customer journey maps and service blueprints
Learn Figma and a collaborative mapping tool
Complete three documented service-design projects
Conduct usability or concept testing and record findings
Complete at least one internship or real-world collaboration
Build a portfolio with clear research and design rationale
Practise presenting a case study to an interview panel
Reset checklist

Start by choosing a familiar service—such as college admissions, healthcare appointments or public transport. Research the people who use it, map their current journey, identify the most important problems, and propose a better service supported by a blueprint and prototype.

The strongest preparation for a Service Designer career is a portfolio that demonstrates research, systems thinking, collaboration and tested improvements. A Design & Innovation Studies degree can provide a valuable foundation, but practical evidence of these abilities will be essential when applying for roles.
